explanation:
## The whole structure

```cpp
std::vector<int> buf(cap, 0);     // cap slots, allocated once
std::size_t count{ 0 };           // how many are in use
```

That is the entire data structure. `buf.size()` is the capacity and never
changes; `count` is the only thing that moves.

```cpp
// push
if (count == buf.size()) { full; }
else { buf[count] = x; ++count; }

// pop
if (count == 0) { empty; }
else { --count; report buf[count]; }

// top
if (count == 0) { empty; }
else { report buf[count - 1]; }
```

## Count, not top-index

With `count` meaning "number of elements":

| | expression | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| next free slot | `buf[count]` | indices `0..count-1` are in use |
| the top element | `buf[count - 1]` | one below the free slot |
| empty | `count == 0` | no subtraction involved |
| full | `count == buf.size()` | no `- 1` involved |

The alternative convention is `int top = -1` pointing at the top element, where
push is `buf[++top] = x` and empty is `top < 0`. It works, and note what it
costs: `top` must be **signed**, because -1 is a legal state. Declare it
`std::size_t` and `top < 0` is never true, so an empty stack reports a top
element - which is the unsigned trap from the search problem, wearing a
different hat.

Both conventions are fine; mixing them is not. If one function treats the
variable as a count and another as an index, every access is off by one and the
symptom is garbage at the boundary rather than a crash.

## Pop does two things, in one order

```cpp
--count;
report buf[count];
```

Decrement first, then read. After `--count`, `count` is the index of what used to
be the top, which is exactly the element being removed. Reading before
decrementing needs `buf[count - 1]` and then a separate `--count`, which is the
same thing written in two steps with one more chance to get the index wrong.

Note that nothing is erased. `buf[count]` still holds the popped value, and the
next push overwrites it. The value is logically gone because `count` says so -
the array is just storage, and the count is the truth. That is worth internalising,
because it is also why "it still worked after I freed it" happens in C.

## Refusing, not overwriting

A full stack **rejects** the push. The alternative - overwrite the top, or wrap
around and clobber the bottom - silently destroys data the caller still believes
is there. A container that cannot satisfy a request should say so.

Reporting it as a return value here, because the protocol asks for a line of
output. In real C++ the three choices are:

- return `bool` and make the caller check - fine, and easy to ignore
- throw an exception - what `std::vector::at` does on a bad index
- treat it as a precondition the caller must not violate - what
  `std::vector::operator[]` does, which is undefined behaviour if you break it

The standard library deliberately offers both of the last two, because bounds
checking is not free and the caller sometimes already knows the index is good.
That is a recurring theme in C++: the unchecked thing exists, is spelled more
conveniently, and is your responsibility.

## Why `std::stack::pop()` returns nothing

```cpp
std::stack<int> s;
s.push(1);
int x = s.top();    // read it
s.pop();            // then remove it - two calls, deliberately
```

A `pop()` that both removed the element and returned it by value would be
impossible to make exception-safe. Returning by value means copying the element
out, and if that copy constructor throws, the element has already been removed
from the container and the copy never arrives - the value is gone, with nowhere
for it to have gone to.

Splitting it means `top()` can throw harmlessly (nothing has changed yet) and
`pop()` cannot throw at all. The API is clumsier and it is the only way to make
the guarantee. C++11 added `std::move` semantics which soften the problem but do
not remove it, since a move constructor is also allowed to throw.

Worth knowing because it is the clearest example of the standard library
choosing a contract over convenience, and because "why is this API so awkward"
usually has an answer like this one.

## Where the stack is in the machine

This is not an analogy - the hardware call stack is this structure. The stack
pointer is `count`, the memory below it is `buf`, a `push` is
`sub rsp, 8; mov [rsp], x` and a `pop` is `mov x, [rsp]; add rsp, 8`.

What the hardware does **not** have is the capacity check. Push past the end of
the stack region and you get a stack overflow - on Linux, the guard page
triggers a SIGSEGV, which is why infinite recursion crashes instead of quietly
corrupting memory. Same structure, same bug, and the only protection is a page
the kernel deliberately left unmapped.

## Allocate once

```cpp
std::vector<int> buf(cap, 0);        // cap elements, all zero
std::vector<int> buf; buf.reserve(cap);   // capacity cap, size 0
```

The first creates `cap` elements you can index immediately. The second reserves
storage but leaves `size()` at 0, so `buf[0]` is out of range even though the
memory exists - and `-fsanitize=address` will catch it as a
container-overflow.

This problem wants the first, because enforcing a fixed capacity by hand is the
exercise. Growing the storage automatically is the next problem in this
sequence.
